Welcome to Eastbourne
by EDITH BOYDELL, President, Eastbourne Branch
I would like to take this opportunity, as President of the Eastbourne Branch, to give you an early welcome to our town of Eastbourne for the Annual Conference to be held in May. Many people who will be coming to the Conference will know Eastbourne and everyone will at least have heard of it.

title: Dukes
brief_context: Influential landowners who planned the layout of Eastbourne.
brief_extract: The new Congress Theatre, at which all large conferences such as ours are held, is admired throughout the world, costing as it did half a million pounds and earning the Civic Trust Award 1963 and the ‘Come to Britain’ Trophy 1963 awarded by the British Travel Association. The impressive lay-out of the town is due chiefly to the fact that it has been the home of the Dukes of Devonshire, who did much to make Eastbourne what it is today, planning it long before Town and Country Planning Acts were ever heard of. The house of the Dukes is known as Compton Place and the late King George V and Queen Mary came often to stay there together with the late King George VII, the Queen Mother and the present Queen and her sister when they were children.

brief_context: His restoration brought more elaborately carved furniture into fashion.
article_title: Who's been sitting in my chair?
brief_extract: The Elizabethan period was one of large furniture, lavishly ornamented, and bulbous legs and columns were frequently used. After the austerities of the Cromwellian period, at the end of the 17th century the Restoration of Charles II brought a swing towards more elaborately carved yet lighter furniture, and walnut came into fashion, together with a taste for veneering. The Great Fire gave scope for new furnishing styles because new furniture was needed for the new brick houses with smaller rooms which were replacing the timber framed houses which had been burnt down.
